title: Bihar-Born Kanishka Narayan Becomes UK's First Cabinet-Level AI Minister
excerpt: Narayan, who moved from Muzaffarpur to Cardiff at age 12, was promoted by PM Andy Burnham just two years after entering Parliament — making Britain one of a handful of countries with a dedicated AI minister at the cabinet table.
body:
• Kanishka Narayan, born in Muzaffarpur, Bihar, was appointed the UK's first Minister for Artificial Intelligence on July 20, a newly created cabinet-attending role under PM Andy Burnham.
  • The 36-year-old Labour MP went from Eton scholarship student to Oxford graduate, Stanford MBA, and investment banker at Lazard before entering Parliament in 2024 as Wales' first ethnic-minority MP.
  • Narayan will oversee the AI Security Institute, a £400 million push to procure British-made AI chips, and £250 million in cloud computing infrastructure expansion.
  • His appointment places the UK alongside the UAE, Canada, and France as countries with dedicated ministerial roles for artificial intelligence.

Kanishka Narayan, a 36-year-old Labour MP born in Muzaffarpur, Bihar, has been elevated to the UK cabinet as the country's first dedicated Minister for Artificial Intelligence, according to an announcement from 10 Downing Street on July 20.

The promotion came during a major cabinet reshuffle by newly appointed Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who dissolved the standalone Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) — a body created by former PM Rishi Sunak in 2023 — and folded its functions into an expanded Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade. Narayan will serve jointly across this new department and the Cabinet Office.

"AI is likely the most significant technology in human history. Its impact will dwarf other things. The best case for it is compelling beyond our dreams: a reindustrialised Britain, stronger national security, public services transformed for the better."

— Kanishka Narayan, UK Minister for AI

From Muzaffarpur to Westminster

Narayan was born in November 1989 into a family with deep roots in Bihar's public life. His paternal grandfather, Krishna Kumar, founded Shri Krishna Jubilee (SKJ) Law College in Muzaffarpur and served as chairman of the district board. Both his parents — Santosh Kumar and Chetna Sinha — studied law at the college before the family relocated, first to Delhi and then to Cardiff, Wales, when Narayan was 12.

His parents worked minimum-wage and night-shift jobs in their early years in Britain, experiences Narayan has credited with shaping his views on social mobility and dignity. He attended a state school in Cardiff before winning a scholarship to Eton College — alma mater of 20 British prime ministers — and went on to study Philosophy, Politics and Economics at Balliol College, Oxford, followed by an MBA at Stanford University, according to Outlook Business.

A Career Spanning Finance, Policy, and Politics

Before entering politics, Narayan built a career across investment banking, venture capital, and government advisory roles. He worked at Lazard, advising major UK companies and government ministries on AI, fintech, and climate-related investments. He later joined European VC firm Atomico and US-based Clocktower Ventures, where he led European operations.

He also served as an economist and senior adviser in the UK government under David Cameron, contributing to drafts of Britain's 25-year environment plan. He joined the Labour Party at 18 and won the Vale of Glamorgan seat in Wales in the July 2024 general election, becoming Wales' first ethnic-minority Member of Parliament — a result the BBC compared to "one of the most significant developments since Lady Megan Lloyd George became the first woman MP from Wales in 1929."

Narayan was appointed Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for AI and Online Safety in September 2025. His promotion to cabinet rank on July 20 came barely two years after he first entered Parliament. He was sworn into the Privy Council the following day, earning the honorific "The Right Honourable" for life, according to official records.

Overseeing Britain's AI Ambitions

As AI minister, Narayan oversees some of the UK's most consequential technology initiatives. These include the AI Security Institute, which evaluates the safety of frontier AI models, a £400 million commitment to procure AI chips from British companies, and a £250 million expansion of cloud computing infrastructure. He has also championed open-source AI development, chairing an Open-Source AI Dev Board and announcing £500,000 in compute resources for public-interest AI tools.

His appointment places Britain alongside the United Arab Emirates, Canada, and France, which have created dedicated ministerial roles for artificial intelligence. The UK is home to leading AI firms including Google DeepMind, Synthesia, ElevenLabs, and Wayve.

Strengthening UK-India Tech Ties

Narayan has actively deepened technology cooperation between the UK and India. In February 2026, he co-led a UK delegation to the India AI Impact Summit in New Delhi, where he held bilateral discussions with Union Minister of State Jitendra Singh on AI collaboration. He later visited Bengaluru — which he called "the beating heart of the world's tech ecosystem" — and returned to his hometown of Patna, where he met JD(U) leader Sanjay Kumar Jha to discuss how AI could benefit agriculture, healthcare, and services in Bihar.

"It's a real pleasure to be here in Bihar. I was born here and I'm back after more than 20 years. You can see a huge amount of progress here."

— Kanishka Narayan, during his visit to Patna in February 2026

What's Next

With his cabinet-level authority, Narayan is expected to shape the UK's approach to AI regulation, semiconductor investment, and the adoption of AI across government services. His dual brief across the Cabinet Office and the business department gives him a cross-cutting role that few technology ministers globally hold. For the Indian diaspora, his rise from a one-bedroom home in Cardiff to the highest levels of the British government adds to a growing list of leaders of Indian origin occupying influential positions in Western policymaking — from the US to Ireland to now, the UK's AI future.
